title: Council Post: The Role Of Precision Timing In The AI Revolution
text:
Markus Lutz is CTO and Founder of SiTime Corporation. He is a MEMS expert, a prolific entrepreneur and inventor who holds over 100 patents.
In an era where artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer a buzzword but a revolutionary force, AI’s synergy with precision timing is foundational for the next wave of technological breakthroughs.
The heartbeat of electronics, precision timing can help to unleash innovation in everything from AI-driven cloud data centers to machine learning in IoT devices to autonomous vehicles. In this article, I'll explore how precision timing has evolved as well as what companies should know about the unique engineering and innovation required for precision timing in AI development.
The Evolution Of Precision Timing
Timekeeping has transcended its traditional role of minute and second tracking in clocks and wristwatches. In today’s era of intelligent, connected devices, precision timing is integral to a plethora of electronic technologies, serving as the vital pulse that ensures optimal system performance, stability and reliability.
Historically, this pulse was regulated by quartz crystal oscillators, akin to the ones used in conventional timepieces. However, the advent of silicon microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) in recent years has marked a significant shift in timing technology. Diminutive MEMS resonators, crafted using advanced semiconductor techniques, are eclipsing quartz technology because of their precision, compactness, cost-effectiveness, lower power consumption and enhanced dependability.
Silicon MEMS timing technologies have revolutionized precision timekeeping by offering devices that are as much as one-twentieth the size of their quartz counterparts. Capable of measuring time to the nanosecond (one-billionth of a second) in some applications, precision timing solutions can open the door to a broader spectrum of use cases.
Superior performance in harsh environmental conditions, including extreme vibrations and temperature fluctuations, has accelerated the adoption of MEMS-based timing across critical sectors like automotive, aerospace, energy and telecommunications.
The Role Of MEMS In AI
MEMS-based precision timing will have an important role in the emerging era of spatial computing and AI.
Data center equipment makers now rely on advanced timing technology to enhance server interconnectivity, network synchronization and performance. As generative AI applications like ChatGPT become more popular and pervasive, the importance of precision timing technology is even more pronounced. Advances in timing technology can contribute to faster, more efficient AI applications, enabling businesses to tackle complex computational challenges, streamline their supply chains and refine customer interactions.
The demand for precision timing is now fueled by AI-driven applications in 5G/6G communications, aerospace and defense, and augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR).
A case in point: Neural networks, the backbone of deep learning (a subset of AI), mimic the complex structure and function of the human brain to process information. These deep learning processes require the rapid, synchronized execution of operations across multiple neural network layers. This is where precision timing comes into play, ensuring harmonious processing at each layer to provide timely, accurate outputs.
The ripple effects of precision timing in AI transcend individual applications. In data centers, the spinal cord of the internet, precision timing streamlines the flow of vast data streams, enabling faster, more reliable server communications crucial for AI computation.
Precision Timing In AI: Implications And Challenges
The integration of AI with precision timing is not only a technical requirement but a strategic imperative. As we venture further into an interconnected, AI-driven world, precision timing will play an even more critical role in synchronizing computer and network resources and ensuring electronics function with efficiency, safety and reliability.
The integration of precision timing in AI, particularly in advanced systems such as supercomputers, also presents unique challenges.
These systems require highly accurate, stable and reliable clocking mechanisms. Precision timing acts as the heartbeat of these electronic systems, but achieving this level of precision in environments characterized by high density and complex integration deviates from traditional design norms.
Engineers must navigate issues such as integrating timing devices in densely packed modules, ensuring functionality under harsh conditions and solving unique density problems. This necessitates innovative engineering approaches, extensive collaboration and iterative problem-solving to ensure optimal system performance and reliability in the ever-evolving landscape of AI technology.
Conclusion
Peering into the future, the proliferation of AI across industries is inevitable. Fields that were once considered traditional, such as agriculture and retail, are now on the cusp of an AI revolution, poised to reap the benefits of precision timing. The ability to process large volumes of data with impeccable timing precision will unlock new horizons in these sectors, from personalized shopping experiences to optimized crop yields.
In the same spirit that ancient civilizations relied on sundials to mark the passage of time while constructing enduring monuments to human creativity, precision timing devices will play an important role in enabling AI-driven technological breakthroughs that will transform and enhance modern society.

title: Can AI Become Your Next CEO?
text:
In the rapidly evolving intersection of AI and corporate leadership, a provocative question is emerging: Can AI step into the shoes of a CEO? The notion may seem far-fetched to some, yet recent developments may suggest that the integration of AI into the highest echelons of management could already be underway. Should this integration become mainstream, it would redefine the essence of modern leadership, unleashing a wave of innovation and transformative changes unlike anything witnessed before.
The Rise Of AI CEOs
The world witnessed a groundbreaking moment as China-based NetDragon Websoft appointed an AI program named Tang Yu as its CEO. This AI-powered virtual humanoid robot was entrusted with supporting decision-making for the company's daily operations. Shortly after the appointment, the company's stock experienced significant growth, surpassing Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index and propelling the company's valuation above $1 billion.
Similarly, a Polish drinks company garnered attention by appointing Mika, the world's first AI human-like robot CEO. Designed to lead critical projects and drive growth, Mika is expected to lead the company towards greater success.
Only time will tell how successful these endeavors will be. Yet, one cannot help but ponder whether these instances are mere isolated experiments or rather indicative of a growing trend that seriously contemplates the role of AI in leadership.
Enhanced Capabilities vs. The Human Touch
A recent poll conducted by edX revealed that an astonishing 49% of CEOs surveyed believe that most, if not all, aspects of their role could be automated or replaced by AI. But is this really the case?
AI's remarkable ability to process vast amounts of data and generate valuable insights has positioned it as a crucial asset for strategic decision-making, a fundamental aspect of any CEO's role. However, according to McKinsey, AI is not yet capable of completely automating the development of strategy. Nevertheless, it can greatly enhance key components of strategy formulation, such as competitive analysis and performance evaluation across different business segments, ultimately leading to improved outcomes. This, in turn, enables faster and more precise decision-making, fostering an agile and efficient approach to leadership.
However, according to Anant Agarwal, the founder of edX, AI excels in technical automation but faces greater challenges in replicating the essential “soft skills” that define a successful CEO. These skills include critical thinking, visioning, creativity, teamwork, collaboration and the ability to inspire and listen among others. In fact, a study published in Harvard Business Review reveals that since 2007, companies seeking C-suite candidates have increasingly emphasized the importance of social (people) skills while downplaying the significance of operational and technical expertise. This goes to show that emotional intelligence and empathy are crucial for effective leadership today.
The CEO - AI Collaboration
Despite AI’s impressive capabilities, it does not operate in isolation. The key to harnessing AI's full potential lies in understanding its strengths and limitations and creating a complementary relationship that plays to both parties' strengths. Leaders provide the crucial human touch, empathy and emotional intelligence that AI currently lacks but is essential for effective leadership. In contrast, AI excels at data analysis and decision-making based on logical algorithms, making it an invaluable resource for CEOs.
Even if AI could fully replicate a CEO's job, it faces ethical, regulatory, societal and trust challenges hindering its mainstream adoption. Clear laws and regulations governing AI in leadership roles are lacking, creating ambiguity over legal responsibility in AI-driven decision-making. Societal acceptance of an AI CEO may be met with resistance due to job loss fears, privacy concerns and mistrust of machine-made decisions.
Echoing this sentiment, Korn Ferry's 2023 research found that CEOs understand the importance of human involvement in decision-making processes based on AI input. In fact, 33% of senior leaders surveyed say they are already experimenting with ways to leverage AI to help boost productivity and operating efficiency. This highlights the recognition that while AI can automate many tasks, humans still play a critical role in ensuring successful outcomes.
So, can AI truly become your next CEO? It may very well happen, but not in the traditional sense. Integrating AI into CEO roles enhances C-suite capabilities, redefining leadership in the digital age. While the human touch remains irreplaceable, the fusion of AI and leadership expertise can usher in a new era of corporate governance where AI acts as a strategic partner in the C-suite.

title: Innovation Beyond AI: Five Big Innovation Themes For 2024 Not About AI
text:
The Economist reports that venture capital firms invested $36 billion in AI in 2023, twice what was spent in 2022. Everything in innovation today is about AI, Gen AI, Deep Learning, and the rest. That’s unsurprising given that the opportunity is now said to be worth $17.7 trillion!
However, that can drown out some of the other interesting trends emerging in my conversations with clients and which I see represented in the Consumer Electronics Show that kicked off in Las Vegas this week. Many of these are AI powered for sure, but they tell us a lot about the competitive battles of the future.
The question I always ask myself is: what problem do they solve for consumers? Sometimes, that is hard to follow.
1. Immersive experiences are coming for us all
We are finally moving toward a world where we interact with devices that are more natural and immersive. NAQI’s “neural earbuds” give us the ability to control devices without speech or touch, just using facial gestures. The initial use case is to open access for people unable to speak or touch, but long-term it can break down barriers for all between the physical and digital world. That we can do this without brain implants is a comfort!
Virtual and augmented reality has generated a lot of cynicism. Google Glass finally found a home in an industrial environment because users took control. Apple believes Vision Pro will be different. Certainly, this is more Apple trying to recover its mojo, but there is some seriously important tech at work. The micro-OLED displays that Apple is using bring us 4k resolution in a 1.3 inch square screen and the next generation micro-LED is another massive leap.
It remains to be seen if it can solve a problem that human beings care about. The same is true of immersive “heads-up displays” that convert a windshield into information hubs and dives cars the ability to project movies. Just because you can, doesn’t mean you should!
2. Find new points of integrated experiences
Apple is not searching for the next gadget; it wants to replicate the control point that it enjoys with the iPhone. This is what enables Apple to capture most of the profit in the phone market without dominating share. They were able to integrate an experience in front of the customer and control everyone else’s access to those consumers.
Michael Jacobides wrote a fabulous HBR article in 2013 explaining how firms that integrate experiences in front of the customer are those that capture the most value. The iPhone is Exhibit A, but the motor car is another where the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) is significantly more profitable than most of the firms in its supply chain (semiconductor companies are a clear exception!).
This makes it interesting that the battle for the car infotainment system is featured in the CES brochure. In “Revving Up the Future: Automotive as the Next Big Tech Battleground,” the author describes the coming battle for the car’s interior, positioning Google and Apple as the likely winners. Here is a new experience for them to integrate.
Then CES pulls a “Rabbit” out of the hat with a reconceived mobile device that seeks to rid us of the need to engage with multiple Apps and services. It aims to turn “large language models” into “large action models” that can read all the different interfaces on our behalf and execute our commands seamlessly. That’s a new level of integration for the user. I first heard about it from my son. Judging from his reaction this is an offer that is likely to resonate with consumers, especially tech nerds him.
3. Automate our lives
Little Leaf, a brand of packaged lettuce, is grown, packed, and shipped without the touch of a single human hand. What’s remarkable is its freshness, flavor and, except for the excessive packaging, that it is more sustainably grown than other brands. This ability to control the process to eliminate waste and improve quality is what intelligent autonomous manufacturing is all about. It seems likely factories of the future will have almost no human touches. What I like about the Little Leaf story is that it demonstrates this can generate customer value with automation. The next frontier will be care robots to solve the elderly care problem, particularly in Japan, where the population imbalance is so acute.
4. Safety in everything
This is a big AI and cyber trend. I think the tech world has finally woken up to how worried consumers are by threats to personal safety. I have been keeping a personal count of the number of advertisements for AI that includes “safe,” or “respect,” or “secure” in the first line of the text. I am up to 25 after one week. This isn’t just a concern for personal safety, but also motivated by professional and commercial considerations. There is a fight back underway against generative AI’s tendency to acquire IP without permission (isn’t that called theft?). Nightshade is a new tool that “poisons” the gen AI models that seek to replicate images ingested without consent. My wife is an artist, so I feel this personally. You shouldn’t be able to build your own works from those of others without full and proper permission.
5. Sustainability is starting to become a value proposition
We are slowly embracing electrification of everything as a way to increase our use of renewables and decrease dependence on carbon intensive fuels. I bought some new Sony earbuds recently and was amazed by how they were packaged entirely without the use of plastics. There are serious firms working on how to make more products recyclable, recognizing the tremendous opportunities to reuse so many of the resources that we currently send to landfills.
At CES, John Deere, the agricultural equipment company, has a stand devoted to its cloud solution that emphasizes its ability to help reduce carbon footprint and improve soil health. It’s been a long-time coming, but the message of sustainability is starting to penetrate everything. I truly believe that only capitalism can move fast enough to solve climate change; let 2024 be a year in which this trend accelerates faster than all others.
We now know that 2023 was not only the hottest on record since before the last Ice Age, but that it significantly bent the growth curve of the last century. That makes sustainability a must for any firms with the remotest concern for the future of humanity. Let’s make opposing sustainability and denying climate change is not only scientific nonsense, but also bad business.
As customers, we need to let firms know that stopped the planet from burning is a problem we expect them to solve.

title: Council Post: Approaching AI In Healthcare: Balancing Promises And Challenges
text:
Cofounder & CEO of PointClickCare, a leading healthcare technology platform enabling meaningful collaboration across the care continuum.
With AI becoming increasingly prevalent, I believe the future of AI applications in healthcare looks promising.
This is a critical moment for healthcare leaders to dive deeper into the potential of generative AI as well as prepare for the challenges that come with AI integration.
Augmenting Human Capabilities With Generative AI
One of the primary advantages of AI in healthcare is its ability to augment human capabilities, allowing clinicians and healthcare staff to operate at the top of their license. By automating repetitive and time-consuming tasks, AI frees up scarce clinical resources, enabling healthcare professionals to concentrate on more critical aspects of patient care.
Virtual assistants and chatbots are just a couple of examples of AI technologies that you can look into to enhance patient engagement and reduce unnecessary visits to healthcare facilities. As a result, overworked and understaffed healthcare teams can lighten their workload and improve their efficiency. This is great news, seeing as the U.S. is currently facing a projected shortage of physicians and increasing rates of burnout.
Through predictive analytics and data-driven insights, AI can help clinicians make more informed decisions and personalize treatment plans to optimize therapies for better patient outcomes. This precision medicine approach not only benefits individual patients but also positively contributes to research and development, advancing value-based care.
Simply put, the more AI-generated insights are provided to clinicians at the point of care, the more efficiently they can make informed care decisions.
Advancing Value-Based Care Through AI
By leveraging machine learning algorithms to analyze data, AI can help your organization identify patterns, risk factors and treatment responses, leading to more precise and personalized care plans. As a result, value-based care models—those focused on improving patient outcomes while controlling costs—can be significantly enhanced.
In value-based care, healthcare providers are incentivized to deliver high-quality care and maintain patient health over the long term. I believe that AI's ability to optimize therapies and treatment plans can more quickly allow providers to achieve these goals.
Insights from AI-driven analytics can enable targeted interventions and identify trends and disparities within patient populations, therefore improving public health initiatives overall.
A Three-Phased Approach To AI Adoption
It’s important to note that AI adoption won't happen overnight. To effectively harness the potential of AI in healthcare, I believe a three-phased approach is necessary.
1. Phase one involves laying the foundation and establishing the infrastructure for AI integration. This includes building robust data repositories, ensuring interoperability between systems and training healthcare staff in AI technology usage. It’s important to gain buy-in from those on the C-suite to the staff in the operating rooms.
2. Phase two focuses on enabling more effective care transitions and proactively mitigating risks before they manifest. By leveraging predictive analytics, AI can identify patients at higher risk for adverse events or readmissions, enabling timely interventions and reducing healthcare costs.
3. Phase three is centered around creating actionable intelligence from vast amounts of digitized information. By transforming data into specific insights, AI promotes cross-collaboration across care settings, enhancing continuity of care and patient experience.
Overcoming Challenges In AI Adoption
While AI offers tremendous potential, it also poses challenges related to privacy, security, regulatory frameworks and ethical considerations. Protecting patient data against data breaches is paramount, and AI developers and healthcare organizations must adhere to strict privacy protocols and comply with regulatory standards.
Further, AI algorithms are trained on large datasets, which may contain biases and reflect existing healthcare disparities. It is crucial to address these biases to ensure that AI-driven decision-making does not perpetuate unfair outcomes. Responsible AI development must involve continuous monitoring and adjustments to algorithms to achieve equitable and just healthcare outcomes for all patients.
It's also important to note that the potential for job displacement due to AI automation is a genuine concern among healthcare professionals. To maintain a skilled and compassionate workforce, support healthcare professionals as they adapt to this changing landscape. Education and upskilling programs can help professionals embrace AI as a valuable tool to enhance their abilities rather than replace them.
A Promising, Still Unfolding Future
The future of AI in healthcare holds tremendous promise for enhancing patient care and advancing value-based medicine. By leveraging generative AI, healthcare professionals can concentrate on critical patient interactions while AI automates repetitive tasks and optimizes treatment plans.
AI-driven analytics also have the potential to improve patient outcomes, promote population health management and enhance value-based care models. Nonetheless, the journey towards the widespread adoption of AI in healthcare is not without challenges.
As technology continues to evolve, embracing AI as a collaborative partner in patient care is important in helping pave the way to maximize healthcare efficiency, empower patients to take charge of their health and ultimately lead to better outcomes for individuals and communities alike.

title: Council Post: 3 Considerations For Manufacturing Leaders Who Are Turning To AI
text:
Donato Montanari is VP and GM, Machine Vision, for Zebra Technologies.
AI is a powerful tool for manufacturing. A recent McKinsey report states AI can potentially create $13 trillion in total economic activity by 2030, with about $1 trillion estimated for the industrial sector alone.
Meanwhile, almost 90% of automotive industry manufacturers surveyed in Zebra’s 2022 Automotive Ecosystem Vision Study intend to engage in digital transformation by 2027. Combined with labor challenges, as 2.1 million manufacturing jobs are predicted to be unfilled by 2030, the industry is ripe for AI—an important step in digitalization.
Like any tool, AI must be applied to the right problem in the right way. Machine vision and deep learning are AI tools that provide an opportunity to solve once unsolvable challenges. One example is visual in-line quality inspection, where defects are hard to detect or unknown.
Here are three considerations about AI for manufacturing decision-makers.
1. Take small steps to apply AI’s vast power.
Define a specific goal, like quality control, and deploy an AI tool one process area at a time. Optical character recognition (OCR)—a focused AI application—is one good starting point.
Deep learning-based OCR can “see” and “read” text on manufacturing parts and be deployed out of the-box—no coding knowledge is required or training of fonts involved. Deep learning-based OCR helps ensure the accuracy of VINs, manufacturing lots, date codes and serial numbers. It can be used to reduce errors or track items moving through a manufacturing line, assuring the right parts move to the right assembly area. Deployment is easy: Simply draw a box around the text you want to read, and your first AI system is deployed in minutes.
Once you define a narrow problem to solve—such as uncovering defects on automobile parts or defective labels—you can determine the best-suited AI tool. With quality inspection, if the defects and their location are known, such as a misplaced label, machine vision is the right tool. If you don’t know what the defects are or their location, like an unexpected chip on a part, machine vision plus deep learning could uncover it.
2. Build AI’s manufacturing brain power.
Before AI can work on a defined problem, it first needs to “learn” about it by “building its brain” or creating a neural network. Think about it as teaching children colors. You show them something red and repeat it until they recognize and comprehend red. Then, you do the same with blue until they understand it too.
The same principle applies to machine vision with deep learning. If you’re teaching AI to recognize a defect in a car part, it needs to repetitively see the defect until it captures and understands it, enabling it to recognize it on the assembly line.
Building AI takes significant computer power (GPUs) and images, which it transforms into a single-minded brain: The newly built brain only knows how to solve the one task it's learned based on the images shown to it. Users create neural networks from their saved images, which are sorted, annotated to build the neural network and used to find defects and anomalies. This makes it critical to have a robust, organized, classified and responsibly annotated repository of images.
This is where many organizations fail: They assign image collection and management to non-qualified workers, resulting in a set of training images that confuses the AI. Back to our child analogy, if we show a child 10 images of red and two images of orange, they'll learn that red and orange are the same color.
A neural network is only as good as the image data it's seen. Say your company manufactures thousands of automotive parts daily, and you don't save images of each part. That’s thousands of opportunities missed to teach a neural network to detect an anomaly or defect. This is where deep learning happens—it converts images into data that AI understands and uses to make decisions.
Remember, images are essential—their datasets are critical for AI to work. When implementing AI, manufacturers must continually build, train and verify the datasets in their AI models.
3. Trust the learning process.
Like humans, AI has a learning curve. On its first quality inspection iteration, AI may catch 75% of defects. The next time, it may catch 80%, and so on, working until it can identify extremely close to 100% of the defects it’s trained to detect. In auto manufacturing, it can detect a part defect the human eye can’t see before it’s installed in a vehicle. In packaging, it can ensure that the accurate number of items are in a carton or that a label is adhered correctly.
No matter how well your operators know a process, unplanned instances arise. You might believe all parts look the same. But when running AI models, you may realize the shade of metal changes or parts look different from batch to batch or supplier to supplier. With continual learning, AI can show experienced quality operators variations that exist in the process, uncovering new improvement opportunities.
AI has made incredible advancements, and the most significant progress in manufacturing is a new algorithm called “anomaly detection.” Previously, for AI to learn about a defect, it would have to see images both of a good part and a defective part. This would have to be repeated for each defect in the defect catalog. In industries like automotive where defects run in the few parts per million scale, generating these images was a challenge.
This challenge is addressed by anomaly detection, which trains only on good images. The AI only needs to "see" images of good parts to detect the difference between good and defective parts. This advancement will lead to more deployments, becoming a standard in manufacturing in the next few years.
The human brain is the greatest processor, but it gets distracted, tired and bored, especially with repetitive manufacturing processes. AI doesn't. Now is the time to take that first small step into an AI application, neural networks and continuous learning—with humans leading the way.

title: Council Post: 5 Questions CEOs Should Ask As They Build AI Partnerships In 2024
text:
Carolyn Parent is CEO of Conveyer, an AI platform that ingests data to generate high-trust, high-accuracy topics and metatags for AI models.
The OpenAI board’s faceplant comes as a timely reminder: Despite premature claims that 2023 was the year AI came of age, the past 12 months have actually been more akin to the toddler years. There’s plenty of enthusiasm and raw potential—but also a lot of stumbling around, messy experimentation and breaking things.
What really matters—and not just for Microsoft, OpenAI and Sam Altman—is what comes next. After a year of growth and investigation, 2024 will be the year in which businesses pivot from trying things to actually doing things with AI and establishing the processes and partnerships needed to scale AI in sustainable and enduring ways.
That makes the next few months critical. As companies move toward rollout and deployment, CEOs will face important decisions about where to commit limited resources. For most companies, that will mean finding the right tech partners to drive their AI initiatives forward.
What CEOs Need To Know
Over the past year, a few tech giants have invested vast sums in building AI models—but most companies have realized that the same buy-versus-build calculus that applied to SaaS solutions applies in the AI era too. Instead of building AI in-house, companies are partnering with specialists that offer expertise and scalable infrastructure.
As CEOs plan for the year ahead, a key challenge will be deciding which companies to partner with. There isn’t much time left to kick the tires, so companies need to make sure the partners and technologies they commit to are fit for the purpose.
Here are five key questions to ask about potential tech partners:
1. How special is their secret sauce?
Many smaller vendors build technologies on top of tech giants’ generative models, and although the results can be impressive, it’s important to ask how much of the value a vendor delivers is inherent to their own product. If they built a wrapper around ChatGPT or Bard, their product—and the advantage you derive from it—can probably be easily replicated by rivals.
The key is to seek companies that have put in the hard work and secured patents for their underlying technology. Proprietary algorithms and original AI innovations beat products that piggyback on third-party models. They also provide more stability and security: As Elon Musk’s Twitter takeover showed, APIs can be switched off, leaving companies that rely on them high and dry.
2. Who’s willing to vouch for their product?
There are a million startups and tech companies to choose from—so how can you figure out which ones to trust? No matter how much due diligence you do with the company, its product and its leadership team, there’s always the risk that you’ll fall victim to salesmanship or hype.
The key test of any company’s ability to deliver lies in its customers. You wouldn’t hire an employee without checking references, and you shouldn’t partner with a tech vendor without speaking to satisfied customers. Large companies kick the tires hardest during procurement processes, so if your vendor is working with Fortune 500 companies or other big players, it's usually a positive sign.
3. Do they pass the Goldilocks test?
The ideal partner is neither too big nor too small. Too small, and you risk your vendor running out of runway or pivoting in a new direction that no longer aligns with your business needs. With new security challenges and regulatory requirements coming down the pike, your vendor also needs the resources and manpower to evolve their product without disruption.
As OpenAI’s jitters show, though, size alone is no guarantee of stability. Moreover, the right solution for your company will often draw on the capabilities of multiple AI models. No single solution is right for all use cases, so getting locked into one big player’s ecosystem early on can leave you with fewer options over time.
4. Do they know your industry?
Many vendors claim their products are industry-agnostic. That makes some sense: Foundational AI models, like stem cells, can evolve in any number of directions. But the process of getting from a foundational model to a viable solution for your company still requires domain expertise.
If you work in fintech, for instance, you need vendors that understand the intricacies of your industry, including any specific regulatory requirements around AI. Look for companies whose leadership teams understand your industry or are already serving leading companies in your space.
5. How much are you worth to them?
More than any other, this is the key question to ask as you plan for the coming year. Your vendor should see you as a valued partner, go above and beyond to keep you happy and quickly resolve any problems you encounter as you deploy their tech.
This is an area in which your procurement process counts for a great deal. You should look for a sales rep who’s responsive and can answer your questions, of course. But you should also look for a company that has already built support infrastructure to help integrate their technologies and reps who proactively work to adapt their offering to drive more value for you and your customers.
Start Planning Now
The next 12 months will be less forgiving than the past year. In the wake of the OpenAI brouhaha, investors and boards will be less inclined to laugh off missteps or sign off on major AI initiatives without ensuring robust processes are in place.
That extends to AI tech partnerships too. If the past year has shown us anything, it’s that data science and AI teams are already overburdened and that new talent is hard to come by. But companies that rush into partnerships without due diligence will get burned.
To bridge the gap between the hype of the past year and the growing need to evolve mature and reliable AI capabilities, CEOs should start planning accordingly—and make sure they’re asking the right questions as they bring new tech partners into the fold.

title: Council Post: AI And Automation: The Future Of Economic Prosperity Lies In Three Crucial Mindset Shifts
text:
CEO and cofounder of Automation Anywhere, a leading global provider of enterprise RPA.
As I prepare for the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos, top of mind are the questions that linger as government and business leaders pivot to make use of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI. According to an EY quarterly survey, 99% of CEOs are making or planning significant investments in generative AI.
Our world has changed substantially since this time last year: With AI and automation, we can now redirect human intellectual capacity to solve major problems globally—not unlike what was accomplished during the Industrial Revolution. These new AI technologies hold the promise of quickly transforming companies and business models to adapt to our rapidly changing world.
Generative AI completes true end-to-end process automation by assisting human judgment and decision-making with smart content generation. Based on hundreds of millions of AI bot transactions, we are seeing companies shift from automating repetitive knowledge work to augmenting thinking and decision-making to create autonomous workflows.
Collaboration between people and AI will help to eliminate fragmented processes and increase cost savings, efficiency and productivity at speeds that were unimaginable just a year ago. One study from Harvard Business School and Boston Consulting Group found that AI can improve a worker’s performance by as much as 40%.
But stakeholders and industry experts are eager to understand how generative AI can catalyze business transformation and economic advancement. In 2024—and beyond—there are three crucial mindset shifts that leaders must embrace to ensure AI drives these changes and accelerates economic growth.
AI isn't the problem. It's the answer.
Multiple problems fall within a leader’s purview—each with a handful of steps required to solve them—and some are treating AI as though it’s one of many difficult challenges they face. What leaders need to understand is that AI isn’t the problem; it’s the solution. It’s a priority for organizations to engage with AI because it will create a solution for many of the problems that leaders need to solve.
Many leaders currently are under pressure from stakeholders to drive innovative solutions for customers, account for economic uncertainty and make progress with various growth and efficiency initiatives. While they might consider AI and its broader impact on the organization as just another problem to solve, leaders should instead see AI as the first step in helping to address these challenges. AI’s adoption and deployment will make it easier to plan for different economic scenarios, free up talent to focus on innovation and offer solutions that they may not have considered.
For instance, one of our customers developed a pilot project in three weeks using AI-based process automation to analyze company data and myriad tax regulations, saving the company $120 million. The company expects that AI-based process automation will help to save $1 billion within a year.
Once harnessed, AI represents a profound business transformation superpower, unlocking the potential of business models, cost structures and customer service and engagement.
AI will define the leaders and the laggards.
Many countries are beginning to face the emerging working-age population and productivity crisis—an increasing gap between the demand for skilled talent and the people available to address it. However, this is not a universally felt crisis; some countries are feeling greater pressure than others. AI may be the great equalizer.
AI, including generative AI, represents a great opportunity to level the playing field for workers. It will reduce tactical, repetitive tasks and allow workers to focus on higher-value, more strategic work. I believe AI will help create a new “system of work” throughout organizations that will assist nearly everyone to do their jobs better.
Regardless of where a country—or company, for that matter—falls in the spectrum of talent needs, AI is a critical tool for economic growth. Like the machines of the Industrial Revolution, AI will become the deciding factor in who leads, who keeps up and who lags.
Responsible AI will counteract its disruption.
At the same time, I fully understand and acknowledge the concerns and risks that AI brings. Responsible AI deployment requires strong governance and security. These technologies exist now, and many companies are deploying AI and automation solutions successfully today. I also strongly believe we will see increasing regulation in the years to come that will help stabilize the safe use of AI within and between countries.
But I acknowledge that AI will impact some people and jobs more than others. Responsible AI puts the onus of anticipating and accounting for this impact on leaders. Affected talent will need to be reskilled, upskilled and redeployed, and this will become one more challenge within the leader’s purview. There are creative ways to approach this, and as the first consideration noted above, AI is not the problem but the solution.
Could the economic benefit that comes from AI be invested in efforts to support those who are impacted? It’s possible that generative AI could become the new oil, in a sense. With AI, companies and countries could follow a similar model as Norway did with its oil revenue, where the wealth generated is invested through the Government Pension Fund Global. The returns benefit the country’s entire population through social services like healthcare, unemployment benefits, pensions, infrastructure projects and education. Companies should consider doing the same for their employees.
The McKinsey Global Institute estimates that "generative AI has the potential to generate value equivalent to $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion in global corporate profits annually." Taking a comparable approach to Norwegian oil revenue with the wealth generated from AI could make a tremendous difference in the average quality of life globally.
Changing the way we work—with the help of AI—necessitates changing our mindsets, starting at the top. In doing so, we can begin to seize the opportunities of AI as a solution to drive business transformation, economic growth and global prosperity.
